chunks: "It depends on the component, but the idea is the same: apply a known stimulus, measure the response, and compute.
Resistance is easiest: a DMM forces a small current and measures the voltage.
For small resistances I use four-wire mode so lead resistance doesn't add, and out of circuit so other paths don't interfere.
For capacitance and inductance, the best bench tool is an LCR meter.
It applies an AC test signal at a chosen frequency and level, measures the complex impedance, and reports the value plus loss, like dissipation factor or ESR.
I pick the frequency near how the part will be used, because the value changes with frequency and bias, and I choose the series or parallel model appropriate to the impedance.
Many DMMs also have a capacitance range, which is fine for rough values. Without an LCR meter I can use simple circuits.
For a capacitor: put it in an RC with a known resistor, drive it with a square wave, and measure the time constant on a scope, so C equals tau over R.
For an inductor: resonate it with a known capacitor and measure the frequency, then L is one over the quantity two pi f squared times C.
Or build a voltage divider with a known resistor and use the amplitude and phase.
For the general impedance versus frequency, up to high frequencies, I'd use an impedance analyzer or a VNA, which gives the self-resonance, ESR and the full picture."
